one_liner: Experimental 2017 compiler from a typed TypeScript subset to WebAssembly via LLVM; up to about 4x over 2017-era browser JS.
what_it_does: You mark functions in a .ts file with the "use speedyjs" directive; the speedyjs CLI or the speedyjs-loader webpack loader compiles them to WebAssembly through LLVM and rewrites the module so JavaScript callers invoke the wasm code, while unmarked functions stay JS. Entry functions called from JS must be declared async and return a Promise. The accepted language is a strict subset: let/const, number/int/boolean, single-element-type arrays, classes without inheritance, top-level functions only; no closures, arrow functions, object literals, any, ==, typeof or instanceof. It needs a custom TypeScript fork (MichaReiser/TypeScript#2.3.3-with-int) for the int type and an LLVM build with the experimental WebAssembly backend.
how_it_is_fast: The TypeScript checker resolves every symbol's static type (plus a 32-bit int type), so the compiler emits LLVM IR on unboxed int32/double values with no type guards, inline caches or deoptimization paths, then runs LLVM opt (O2 by default, O3 in the benchmark), s2wasm and optionally Binaryen wasm-opt. Arrays live in a C++ runtime (built with Emscripten) as contiguous typed storage, and the default 'unsafe' runtime removes their bounds checks. There is no tracing GC: by default everything allocated is freed when the entry function returns (a 'heap nuke'), or on demand through speedyJsGc (dlmalloc malloc_inspect_all + bulk_free).
when_to_use: As a research reference for typed-subset JavaScript-to-WebAssembly compilation (VMIL 2017, Reiser and Blaeser), including its committed per-browser result files.
Integer-heavy recursive or loop kernels that already fit the subset: fib about 3.5x (Chrome 58) and 2.9x (Firefox 53), nsieve 2.7x and 4.0x, isPrime about 3.1x in Chrome only (1.06x in Firefox).
Studying how bounds checks and GC accounting change JS-vs-wasm comparisons: the repo has safe and unsafe runs from the same day (results/20170504-safe.json and 20170504.json).
Reproducing the 2017 numbers with the author's prebuilt Ubuntu VM rather than a modern toolchain.
when_not_to_use: Any production or new project: archived 2023-04-22, last commit 2017-10-23, the author called it very experimental, and npm install fails on current toolchains (issue #61: llvm-node 2.1.0 does not build against LLVM 10.0.0 and Node 14.17.0).
Code that needs strings, closures, arrow functions, object literals, inheritance or dynamic typing; none are supported.

Floating-point or comparison-bound kernels: tspDouble, tspArrayDouble, doubleAdd and doubleCompare stay at 0.96x to 1.02x, intCompare is 0.94x in Firefox, and nbody is slower than JS (0.81x Chrome 59, 0.92x Firefox 53).

When memory safety matters: the default and benchmarked unsafe mode has no array bounds checks, and with the safe runtime array kernels fall below plain JS (Chrome 58: simjs 0.60x, mergeSort 0.73x, arrayReverse 0.24x).
When a maintained TypeScript-like wasm language is an option: the AssemblyScript-based siblings or MoonBit cover the same niche with active toolchains.

integration.form: module (npm speedyjs-compiler 0.0.19 CLI plus speedyjs-loader webpack loader)
integration.dependencies: TypeScript fork MichaReiser/TypeScript#2.3.3-with-int, llvm-node ^2.0.3, an LLVM install with the experimental WebAssembly target (LLVM_CONFIG), Binaryen s2wasm/wasm-opt, the Emscripten-built speedyjs-runtime
integration.min_toolchain: 2017-era LLVM with the experimental WebAssembly backend and a Node version llvm-node 2.x builds against; llvm-node 2.1.0 fails with LLVM 10.0.0 and Node 14.17.0 (issue #61)
integration.platforms: Output runs in WebAssembly MVP browsers (results recorded for Chrome 58 to 61, Firefox 53 and 55, Safari 10.2 on macOS 10.12); compiler host documented for Linux/macOS (prebuilt Ubuntu VM), Windows not documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — existing JS/TS functions compile only if they already fit the subset; entry functions must become async, and array semantics differ from JS (out-of-bounds reads return the element default instead of undefined; out-of-bounds writes throw in safe mode and are unchecked in unsafe mode)

gotchas: Harness: packages/benchmark/run-benchmarks.js builds the Speedy.js side with {unsafe: true, optimizationLevel: 3, binaryenOpt: true, disableHeapNukeOnExit: true, exportGc: true}, so the record's 'default compiler options' is wrong (defaults are O2 and binaryenOpt false), and unsafe links the runtime built with -DUNSAFE, which drops array bounds checks. The repo's own same-day results show the gains depend on it: safe mode (20170504-safe.json) gives simjs 0.60x, mergeSort 0.73x, mergeSortInt 0.77x and arrayReverse 0.24x against JS in Chrome 58 (simjs 0.42x and arrayReverse 0.72x in Firefox 53), against 1.05x, 1.31x, 1.35x and 1.76x unsafe (20170504.json).

Harness: with disableHeapNukeOnExit the wasm kernels never free memory inside the timed loop; speedyJsGc runs in benchmark.js's onCycle hook between cycles, while the JS engines' GC runs inside the timed region, which favours the allocating kernels (mergeSort, mergeSortInt, arrayReverse, simjs, the tsp cases).

Selective reporting: the 2017-06-06 run that the doc/benchmark-results.pdf table comes from (Chrome 59, Firefox 53) also contains nbody, where Speedy.js loses to JS (0.81x and 0.92x) and to Emscripten (0.81x and 0.86x), plus factorize; the PDF shows 8 of its 16 kernels, and the README chart is an earlier 14-kernel run (results/20170528.json, Chrome 58). The Emscripten nsieve baseline uses bit-packed std::vector<bool>, so Speedy.js's 1.78x lead over Emscripten on nsieve in Chrome is not like-for-like.

speedyjs-compiler-options.ts documents defaults the code does not use: totalStack is documented as 5 MB but set to 5*1024*104 bytes (about 520 KB) with no stack-overflow check, and binaryenOpt (true vs false), optimizationLevel (3 vs 2) and globalBase (1024 vs 8) also differ, so deep recursion can silently overrun the stack.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only to study or cite the design; for new code the AssemblyScript-based siblings (as-proto, as-str, galois) or MoonBit offer a maintained TypeScript-like path to wasm, and Cheerp covers C++ sources. Its one distinguishing point is compiling marked functions inside an otherwise-JS module through LLVM, which those siblings do not do.
verified_claims_summary: benchmark.js ops/s of 14 small kernels compiled by Speedy.js (unsafe runtime, LLVM O3 plus Binaryen) against the same TypeScript run as JS, in Chrome 58.0.3029.110 and Firefox 53.0 on macOS 10.12 (Intel Mac user agent, no CPU model recorded) (README chart, results/20170528.json): fib about 3.5x and 2.9x, isPrime 3.1x and 1.06x, nsieve 2.7x and 4.0x, arrayReverse 0.91x and 4.4x, merge sort 1.3x to 1.6x, and the floating-point kernels at about 1.0x. Emscripten -O3 C++ builds of the same kernels land within a few percent of Speedy.js on most of them, so the gain is wasm over 2017 JIT output, not a better code generator.
status_note: Archived 2023-04-22 (last commit 2017-10-23), MIT; not installable on current toolchains (issue #61), so it is reference material only; the headline speedups come from a first-party 2017 harness that runs the wasm side without bounds checks, keeps its frees out of the timed loop, and leaves out nbody, the kernel where Speedy.js loses to JS.
